paras: The killing of Henry Ebenhack was the fatal shooting of a Wichita, Kansas, police officer by John "Jack" Thornton of McMahan's patrol, on the morning of September 24, 1888, while Ebenhack and another officer were taking Thornton under arrest. A coroner's jury found the next day that Thornton had fired "without felonious intent, but under great provocation and danger of bodily injury," although a justice of the peace later held him to answer a charge of murder. A wire brief printed in Washington added that Thornton "barely escaped lynching" before he was jailed, a claim that does not appear in the local reports.

Besides its regular police, Wichita had a patrol under Chief McMahan whose men were expected to visit "a joint or a house of prostitution" in search of evidence. The Wichita Eagle described Thornton, a former hack driver and coachman, as "quiet and orderly." Ebenhack, about 28 years old, had served on the regular force since November 1887 and had recently married.
Testimony at the inquest pointed to friction between the two men: one witness said Ebenhack complained that Thornton had been reporting him and spoke of wanting to "play even."

According to Officer S. A. Hartzell, Ebenhack asked him that morning to help "pull" Thornton from what the Eagle called a "bawdy house" at Central and Main. The officers found Thornton there in uniform; he said he had come "on business for McMahan," and McMahan later testified that he had sent Thornton to visit two women in search of information. As the three men walked toward the station, Thornton said Ebenhack "had it in for him," angry words followed, and near the Christian church on Market Street Thornton began rolling up his sleeves.

Ebenhack then struck him over the head, with what the Eagle called the butt end of a whip, and Hartzell grabbed Thornton around the waist. Thornton drew a revolver and fired three shots around Hartzell's body, and the city physician testified that the first passed through Ebenhack's heart. Ebenhack staggered into the street and died, while Thornton handed his two revolvers to Hartzell, said he was ready to die, and was taken to the city prison.

Coroner O. F. Pearcey convened a six-man jury that afternoon, and so many men surrounded the courthouse and pressed into the room that the jurors had the spectators cleared. Bystanders largely agreed with Hartzell, and McMahan told the jury that the patrol and the police were "on good terms."

On September 25 the jury returned its finding of provocation and danger of bodily injury, and the Eagle reported that the jurors, three of them friends of Ebenhack, regarded the arrest as "a scheme to disgrace Thornton." Thornton's preliminary hearing before Justice Walker opened on October 3 and ended the next day with Thornton held in $2,000 bond to answer a charge of murder. Four men furnished the bond and he was released, and no report of a trial was found.

The Wichita Eagle covered the case in detail, printing inquest testimony at length under the headlines "SHOT DEAD" and "THE CORONER'S VERDICT" and following the hearing in its court column. While calling both men brave officers, its reporting leaned toward Thornton, stating that the evidence "was very strongly in favor of Thornton" and that the verdict was seen on the streets as the only one possible.

Outside Wichita the story ran as a short item: the Washington Critic's wire brief, headed "Fatal Quarrel Between Policemen," blamed "a natural rivalry and antipathy between the two forces" and an old grudge, and it alone mentioned a lynching threat. The Barton County Democrat on October 4 and the Phillipsburg Herald on October 26 summarized the arrest, the blow with a cane and the shooting without mentioning a mob. None of these papers named the race of either man.

The lynching threat rests on the Critic's brief alone; the Eagle's testimony-based account has Thornton surrendering his revolvers and going to the city prison with no crowd mentioned. Details also varied: the Phillipsburg Herald counted two shots where others counted three, and Ebenhack's weapon was a whip handle, a cane or a "billy."

reader.title: Killing of Henry Ebenhack
bases: The episode is the fatal shooting of a regular police officer by a patrolman he was arresting, after a quarrel and a blow (A3, A6); the only mob element is one wire clause saying Thornton 'barely escaped lynching' (A2).

No one was killed by a group: Ebenhack was shot by one man, Thornton, in a quarrel (A3, A6), and Thornton, the man said to have been threatened with lynching, was jailed, released on bond and not harmed (A2, A3, A9).

The shooting is corroborated by the local Eagle and three other papers (A3, A6, A7, A10), but the lynching threat appears only in the Washington Critic's wire brief (A2), and the Eagle's sworn-testimony account of the arrest mentions no mob (A3).

The Washington Critic ran a short wire item headed 'Fatal Quarrel Between Policemen,' the only report of a lynching threat.
Kansas news columns gave brief factual summaries without comment.

Henry Ebenhack (also Ebenback, Ebenbach), regular police officer, killed; John (Jack) Thornton of McMahan's patrol, the shooter, said by one wire report to have barely escaped lynching
Thornton shot and killed Officer Ebenhack; held to answer a charge of murder
Shooting: John Thornton alone. Lynching threat: unnamed, no crowd described
